decks.title: Angles and Trigonometric Functions - Part 1: Angles, radian measure and the unit circle
goals: Convert angles between degrees and radians
Find the arc length and the area of a sector
Define sine and cosine with the unit circle and use the basic identities
Find all six ratios from one ratio and the quadrant

slides.heading: Angles and Trigonometric Functions, Part 1
slides.body_md: From turning through an angle to the coordinates of a point on a circle.

visual.alt: A circle with its centre O. A radius from O to a point P on the circle makes an angle called theta with the positive horizontal axis; a dashed line drops from P to the horizontal axis.
visual.caption: Turning from the positive $x$-axis through $\theta$ reaches the point $P$.

slides.narration: Welcome to the chapter on angles and trigonometric functions. A turning door, a spinning wheel and a swinging pendulum all involve angles. In this part you will measure angles in degrees and in radians, find the length of an arc and the area of a sector, and then define sine and cosine as coordinates of a point on the unit circle.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
slides.body_md: By the end of this part you can:
bullets: Convert angles between degrees and radians
Find arc length and sector area
Define the functions from the unit circle
Find all six ratios from one ratio and the quadrant

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: angles and turning, degrees and radians, arc length and sector area, the unit circle, and signs together with the basic identities.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Here is the plan. First we meet positive and negative angles and the two units for measuring them. Then we use radians to find arc lengths and sector areas. Finally we place a point on the unit circle, read off sine and cosine, and learn the identities and the signs in each quadrant.

slides.heading: Positive and negative angles
slides.body_md: An angle is made by turning an initial ray about its vertex. **Anticlockwise** turns give **positive** angles and **clockwise** turns give **negative** angles. Angles that end on the same ray are **coterminal**.

visual.alt: A circle with centre O and two radii, one to a point P above the horizontal axis and one to a point N below it. The angle to P is marked plus 50 degrees, turned anticlockwise, and the angle to N is marked minus 50 degrees, turned clockwise from the positive horizontal axis.
visual.caption: Anticlockwise gives $+50^\circ$; clockwise gives $-50^\circ$.

slides.narration: An angle is formed by turning a ray about its end point. Turning anticlockwise gives a positive angle. Turning clockwise gives a negative angle. Here the same size of turn is shown both ways, plus fifty degrees and minus fifty degrees. Two angles that finish on the same ray are called coterminal, and they differ by whole turns.

slides.heading: Degrees and radians
slides.body_md: One full turn is $360^\circ$. A **radian** is the angle at the centre that cuts off an arc equal in length to the radius. In general $\theta = \dfrac{l}{r}$.

visual.alt: A circle sector with centre O and radius r. The arc between the two radii is twice as long as the radius, so the angle at the centre is 2 radians, about 115 degrees.
visual.caption: An arc of length $2r$ subtends $2$ radians.

slides.narration: There are two common units. A degree is one three hundred and sixtieth of a full turn. A radian is defined by a circle itself: it is the angle at the centre that cuts off an arc as long as the radius. In the picture the arc is twice the radius, so the angle is two radians. In general the angle in radians is the arc divided by the radius.

slides.heading: Converting between the units
slides.body_md: A full turn is $2\pi$ radians, so $\pi$ radians $= 180^\circ$.

visual.alt: Table converting common angles from degrees to radians, from 30 degrees equal to pi over 6 up to 360 degrees equal to 2 pi.
visual.caption: $\pi$ radians $= 180^\circ$, so $1^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{180}$ radian and $1$ radian $= \dfrac{180}{\pi}$ degrees.

slides.narration: The circumference of a circle is two pi times the radius, so one full turn is two pi radians, and a half turn is pi radians, equal to one hundred and eighty degrees. To change degrees into radians multiply by pi over one hundred and eighty. To change radians into degrees multiply by one hundred and eighty over pi. The table lists the angles you will use most often.

slides.heading: Quick check: radians to degrees
slides.body_md: Convert an angle given as a fraction of pi into degrees.
slides.narration: Replace pi by one hundred and eighty degrees and simplify the fraction.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: four conversions
slides.body_md: Convert $75^\circ$ and $-210^\circ$ to radians, and $\dfrac{13\pi}{18}$ rad and $2.5$ rad to degrees.

visual.alt: Worked example 1 table: 75 degrees equals 5 pi over 12 radians; minus 210 degrees equals minus 7 pi over 6 radians; 13 pi over 18 radians equals 130 degrees; 2.5 radians equals about 143.24 degrees.
visual.caption: Multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$ going in, by $\dfrac{180}{\pi}$ coming back.

slides.narration: To go from degrees to radians multiply by pi over one hundred and eighty and cancel. Seventy five degrees becomes five pi over twelve. Minus two hundred and ten degrees becomes minus seven pi over six, keeping the sign. To go back, multiply by one hundred and eighty over pi. Thirteen pi over eighteen is one hundred and thirty degrees, and two and a half radians is about one hundred and forty three point two four degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: terminal sides
slides.body_md: Decide whether a positive and a negative angle end on the same ray.
slides.narration: Add or subtract whole turns until both angles lie between zero and three hundred and sixty degrees.

slides.heading: Arc length
slides.body_md: In a circle of radius $r$, an arc that subtends the angle $\theta$ at the centre has length $l = r\theta$, **provided $\theta$ is in radians**.

visual.alt: A circle sector with centre O, radius r and central angle theta. The curved boundary between the two radii has length l, which equals r times theta when theta is measured in radians.
visual.caption: $l = r\theta$ when $\theta$ is in radians.

slides.narration: Since the angle in radians is the arc divided by the radius, the arc length is the radius times the angle. This simple formula works only when the angle is in radians. If the angle is given in degrees, convert it first, or use pi times r times theta over one hundred and eighty.

slides.heading: Area of a sector
slides.body_md: A sector with radius $r$ and angle $\theta$ (radians) has area $A = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}rl$.

visual.alt: Table of sector formulae: arc length is r theta with theta in radians or pi r theta over 180 with theta in degrees; area is half r squared theta or pi r squared theta over 360; and in terms of the arc the area is half r times l.
visual.caption: Same facts in two units; radians give the shorter formulas.

slides.narration: A sector is a fraction of the whole disc. The fraction is theta over two pi, so the area is theta over two pi times pi r squared, which simplifies to half r squared theta. Replacing r theta by the arc length gives the equally useful form, half times radius times arc. The table shows both units side by side.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the beam of a lamp
slides.body_md: A lamp in an imagined lighthouse lights a sector of sea of radius $21$ km through $80^\circ$. Find the length of the outer boundary and the area lit. Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

visual.alt: Worked example 2 table for a sector of radius 21 kilometres and angle 80 degrees: the angle is 4 pi over 9 radians, the arc is 28 pi over 3, about 29.33 kilometres, and the area is 98 pi, about 308 square kilometres, using pi equal to 22 over 7.
visual.caption: Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

slides.narration: First change eighty degrees to radians: four pi over nine. The arc is twenty one times four pi over nine, which is twenty eight pi over three, about twenty nine point three three kilometres. The area is half times four hundred and forty one times four pi over nine, which is ninety eight pi. Using twenty two over seven for pi, that is three hundred and eight square kilometres.

slides.heading: Quick check: an arc from a radian angle
slides.body_md: Find an arc length from a radius and an angle in radians.
slides.narration: The angle is already in radians, so multiply it by the radius.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: arc and area given
slides.body_md: A sector has an arc of length $12$ cm and an area of $36$ cm$^2$. Find the radius, the angle in radians and the angle in degrees.

visual.alt: Worked example 3 table: from an arc of 12 centimetres and an area of 36 square centimetres, the radius is 6 centimetres, the angle is 2 radians, which is about 114.59 degrees.
visual.caption: Both $l$ and $A$ given: solve for $r$ first.

slides.narration: When both the arc and the area are given, use the area formula with the arc first. Half times r times twelve equals thirty six, so r is six centimetres. Then the angle is the arc over the radius, twelve over six, which is two radians. In degrees that is about one hundred and fourteen point five nine degrees.

slides.heading: The unit circle definition
slides.body_md: Turn through $\theta$ from the point $(1, 0)$ on the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ and reach $P$. Then $\cos\theta$ is the $x$-coordinate of $P$ and $\sin\theta$ is its $y$-coordinate.

visual.alt: The unit circle with a point P in the second quadrant at an angle theta of 125 degrees from the positive horizontal axis, with a dashed vertical line down to the horizontal axis. The coordinates of P are cosine theta and sine theta.
visual.caption: $P(\theta) = (\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta)$; here $\theta = 125^\circ$.

slides.narration: Now we define the functions for any angle. Take the circle of radius one about the origin. Start at the point one, zero and turn through the angle theta. The point you reach has two coordinates. The horizontal coordinate is cosine theta and the vertical coordinate is sine theta. Tangent is sine over cosine, and the other three are reciprocals.

slides.heading: Basic identities
slides.body_md: The point $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ lies on $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, so $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ for **every** real $\theta$.

visual.alt: Table of the basic relations: sine squared plus cosine squared equals one for all angles; one plus tangent squared equals secant squared where cosine is not zero; one plus cotangent squared equals cosecant squared where sine is not zero; tangent and cotangent as quotients; cosecant and secant as reciprocals.
visual.caption: All five follow from the unit circle.

slides.narration: Because the point lies on the unit circle, its coordinates satisfy x squared plus y squared equals one. That gives the main identity: sine squared plus cosine squared equals one, true for every angle. Dividing by cosine squared or by sine squared gives the two companion identities, which hold only where the denominators are not zero. Tangent, cotangent, secant and cosecant are quotients or reciprocals.

slides.heading: Quick check: an identity at a special angle
slides.body_md: Test the main identity where tangent is undefined.
slides.narration: Does the main identity need any division? Compare with the companion identities.

slides.heading: Signs in the four quadrants
slides.body_md: The signs follow from the coordinates of $P$: cosine is the $x$-coordinate, sine is the $y$-coordinate. In quadrant I all six are positive; in II sine and cosecant; in III tangent and cotangent; in IV cosine and secant.

visual.alt: The four quadrants of the coordinate plane with the functions that are positive in each: all six in the first quadrant, sine and cosecant in the second, tangent and cotangent in the third, and cosine and secant in the fourth.
visual.caption: Positive functions by quadrant; the rest are negative.

slides.narration: The signs depend on where the point lies. In the first quadrant both coordinates are positive, so all six functions are positive. In the second quadrant only the vertical coordinate is positive, so sine and its reciprocal are positive. In the third quadrant both are negative, so their ratio, tangent, is positive. In the fourth quadrant only cosine and secant are positive.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: all six from one
slides.body_md: If $\cos\theta = \dfrac{20}{29}$ and $\theta$ lies in the fourth quadrant, find the other five functions.

rows: $-\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{400}{841}}$, sine is negative in quadrant IV

visual.alt: Worked example 4 table for cosine theta equal to 20 over 29 in the fourth quadrant: sine is minus 21 over 29, tangent minus 21 over 20, cosecant minus 29 over 21, secant 29 over 20 and cotangent minus 20 over 21.
visual.caption: Given $\cos\theta = \dfrac{20}{29}$, $\theta$ in quadrant IV.

slides.narration: Use the main identity to find the size of sine. Sine squared is one minus four hundred over eight hundred and forty one, which is four hundred and forty one over eight hundred and forty one, so sine has size twenty one over twenty nine. In the fourth quadrant sine is negative. The tangent follows by division, and the reciprocals by inverting.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: proving an identity
slides.body_md: Prove that $\dfrac{\sin\theta}{1 + \cos\theta} + \dfrac{1 + \cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = 2\operatorname{cosec}\theta$.

visual.alt: Worked example 5 table proving that sine over one plus cosine, plus one plus cosine over sine, equals 2 cosecant: combine over a common denominator, expand, use sine squared plus cosine squared equals one, cancel one plus cosine, and write the result as 2 cosecant theta.
visual.caption: Start from the left side only.

slides.narration: Work on the left side only. Put both fractions over the common denominator sine times one plus cosine. The numerator is sine squared plus the square of one plus cosine. Expanding and using the main identity turns it into two plus two cosine. Factor out two, cancel one plus cosine, and what remains is two over sine, which is two cosecant theta.

slides.heading: Summary

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: a radian is arc divided by radius, giving arc length r theta and sector area half r squared theta; the unit circle defines cosine and sine as the coordinates of P; the identities and quadrant signs follow.
visual.caption: Part 1 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. A radian is arc divided by radius, and pi radians make one hundred and eighty degrees. With the angle in radians the arc is r theta and the sector area is half r squared theta. On the unit circle cosine and sine are the coordinates of the point. They satisfy the main identity, and their signs depend on the quadrant.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name the quadrant before choosing a sign
In a proof, work on one side and state the identity used

headers: How ISC marks are usually given
rows: start from one side 1, key identity 1, finish 1

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 1: conversions earn a mark each, arc and sector questions award the radian angle, the formula and the answer, finding all ratios awards the missing ratio, the signs and the rest, and proofs award the start, the key identity and the finish.
visual.caption: Write the quadrant before choosing a sign.

slides.narration: In the examination, change degrees to radians before using the arc formula. When finding a ratio from another, decide the quadrant first and then choose the sign. In a proof, start from one side only and name the identity you use at each step. And take care with notation: sine squared theta means the square of sine theta.

decks.title: Angles and Trigonometric Functions - Part 2: Any angle, allied angles and graphs
goals: Evaluate the functions at angles of any size using reduction and allied angles
State the domain, range and period of all six functions
Sketch the graphs of the six functions

slides.heading: Angles and Trigonometric Functions, Part 2
slides.body_md: Values at any angle, and the six graphs.

visual.alt: The unit circle with four points: P at an angle theta in the first quadrant, R in the second quadrant, S in the third and T in the fourth. The four points are mirror images of one another in the two axes and the centre.
visual.caption: Four angles built from one acute angle $\theta$ meet the circle at mirror-image points.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. One acute angle and its mirror images give four points on the unit circle, and that picture explains all the allied angle rules. In this part you will evaluate the functions at large and negative angles, simplify expressions, and learn the domain, range, period and graph of each of the six functions.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
slides.body_md: By the end of this part you can:
bullets: Reduce any angle by whole turns
Use allied angles to find exact values

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: angles beyond one turn, allied angles, domain and range, and the graphs of the six functions.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: Here is the plan. We start by removing whole turns from large angles. Then we study allied angles, which are the angles ninety degrees, one hundred and eighty degrees and so on, plus or minus a small angle. Finally we study each function as a whole: where it is defined, what values it takes, how often it repeats, and what its graph looks like.

slides.heading: Angles of any size
slides.body_md: A full turn brings a point back to where it started, so $P(\theta + 360^\circ n) = P(\theta)$ and every function has the same value at coterminal angles.

visual.alt: Table reducing large angles by whole turns: 765 degrees is 2 turns plus 45 degrees in the first quadrant; minus 840 degrees is minus 3 turns plus 240 degrees in the third; 1230 degrees is 3 turns plus 150 degrees in the second; 2100 degrees is 5 turns plus 300 degrees in the fourth.
visual.caption: Adding or removing whole turns does not change any trigonometric value.

slides.narration: Adding or removing a whole turn puts the point back in the same place, so all six functions take the same values. To handle a large or negative angle, remove whole turns until the angle lies between zero and three hundred and sixty degrees. Then find its quadrant. The table shows four angles reduced in this way.

slides.heading: Values at the standard angles
slides.body_md: Memorise the sine row: $0, \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, 1$. Cosine is the same row backwards; the rest follow by division and reciprocals.

visual.alt: Table of the six trigonometric functions at 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees. Sine runs 0, one half, root 2 over 2, root 3 over 2, 1; cosine runs the other way; tangent runs 0, root 3 over 3, 1, root 3, not defined; and the reciprocal functions follow, with cosecant not defined at 0 and secant and cotangent not defined where their denominators vanish.
visual.caption: Learn sine; the rest follow from it.

slides.narration: These are the values you must know. Sine at zero, thirty, forty five, sixty and ninety degrees is zero, one half, root two over two, root three over two, and one. Cosine runs through the same numbers in reverse. Tangent is sine divided by cosine, and the other three are reciprocals. Where a denominator is zero the function is not defined.

slides.heading: Allied angles: the negative of an angle
slides.body_md: The point for $-\theta$ is the mirror image of the point for $\theta$ in the $x$-axis. So $\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta$ and $\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta$: cosine is **even**, sine and tangent are **odd**.

visual.alt: The unit circle with a point P at angle theta above the horizontal axis and its mirror image at angle minus theta below it, joined by a dashed vertical line. The two points have the same horizontal position and opposite heights.
visual.caption: $P(-\theta)$ is the mirror image of $P(\theta)$ in the $x$-axis: $\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta$, $\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta$.

slides.narration: Turning by minus theta gives the mirror image of the point for theta in the horizontal axis. The horizontal coordinate stays the same, so cosine is an even function. The vertical coordinate changes sign, so sine is odd, and tangent, being sine over cosine, is odd as well.

slides.heading: Allied angles: half turns
slides.body_md: $P(\pi - \theta)$ is the mirror image of $P(\theta)$ in the $y$-axis: sine unchanged, cosine reversed. $P(\pi + \theta)$ is the opposite end of the diameter: both reversed.

visual.alt: The unit circle with P at angle theta, R at pi minus theta in the second quadrant and S at pi plus theta in the third quadrant. R is the mirror image of P in the vertical axis, and S is the point diametrically opposite P.
visual.caption: $P(\pi - \theta)$: mirror in the $y$-axis. $P(\pi + \theta)$: opposite end of the diameter.

slides.narration: The point for pi minus theta is the mirror image of the point for theta in the vertical axis. It has the same height, so the sine is unchanged, and the opposite horizontal position, so the cosine changes sign. The point for pi plus theta is directly opposite through the centre, so both coordinates change sign, and the tangent stays the same.

slides.heading: The allied-angle table
slides.body_md: For an **acute** $\theta$, the eight related angles give these results. The signs come from the quadrant.

visual.alt: Table of allied-angle results. Minus theta: minus sine theta, cosine theta, minus tangent theta. 90 degrees minus theta: cosine, sine, cotangent. 90 plus theta: cosine, minus sine, minus cotangent. 180 minus theta: sine, minus cosine, minus tangent. 180 plus theta: minus sine, minus cosine, tangent. 270 minus theta: minus cosine, minus sine, cotangent. 270 plus theta: minus cosine, sine, minus cotangent. 360 minus theta: minus sine, cosine, minus tangent.
visual.caption: Here $\theta$ is treated as an acute angle.

slides.narration: Here are all the allied results in one table. For ninety and two hundred and seventy degrees the function changes into its partner, sine into cosine and tangent into cotangent. For one hundred and eighty and three hundred and sixty degrees the function stays the same. In every case the sign is the sign that the original function has in the quadrant reached.

slides.heading: A rule that works every time
slides.body_md: Write the angle as a multiple of $90^\circ$ plus or minus an acute $\theta$, decide whether to swap, then fix the sign by the quadrant.

nodes.label: $k$ odd: swap sine with cosine, tangent with cotangent
Sign from the quadrant of the original angle

visual.alt: Flow chart for allied angles: write the angle as a multiple of 90 degrees plus or minus an acute angle theta; if the multiple is even keep the function, if it is odd swap sine with cosine and tangent with cotangent; then take the sign that the original function has in the quadrant of the original angle.
visual.caption: Even keeps, odd swaps; the quadrant gives the sign.

slides.narration: Here is a rule that always works. Write the angle as a multiple of ninety degrees plus or minus a small acute angle. If the multiple is even, keep the same function. If it is odd, swap sine with cosine, and tangent with cotangent. Finally decide the sign by asking which quadrant the original angle is in and what sign the original function has there.

slides.heading: Quick check: a reciprocal at a special angle
slides.body_md: Evaluate cosecant at a negative quadrantal angle.
slides.narration: Find the sine first, then take its reciprocal.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: exact values of large angles
slides.body_md: Find the exact values of $\sin\left(-\dfrac{11\pi}{3}\right)$, $\tan 1290^\circ$ and $\cos 1020^\circ$.

visual.alt: Worked example 1 table: sine of minus 11 pi over 3 reduces to sine of 60 degrees, which is root 3 over 2; tangent of 1290 degrees reduces to tangent of 210 degrees, which equals tangent of 30 degrees, root 3 over 3; cosine of 1020 degrees reduces to cosine of 300 degrees, which equals cosine of 60 degrees, one half.
visual.caption: Remove whole turns, then use the allied-angle rule.

slides.narration: For each angle, remove whole turns first. Minus eleven pi over three is minus six hundred and sixty degrees, and adding two turns gives sixty degrees, so the sine is root three over two. One thousand two hundred and ninety degrees reduces to two hundred and ten, where tangent is positive and equals tangent of thirty. One thousand and twenty reduces to three hundred, where cosine is positive and equals one half.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: simplifying with allied angles
slides.body_md: Simplify $\dfrac{\sin(\pi - x)\cos\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + x\right)}{\tan(\pi + x)\cot\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right)}$.

rows: odd multiple: swap; quadrant IV, cosine positive
even multiple: keep; quadrant III, tangent positive

visual.alt: Worked example 2 table simplifying sine of pi minus x times cosine of 3 pi over 2 plus x, divided by tangent of pi plus x times cotangent of pi over 2 minus x: the factors become sine x, sine x, tangent x and tangent x, so the expression equals cosine squared x.
visual.caption: Replace each factor, then simplify.

slides.narration: Replace each factor using the rule. Sine of pi minus x is sine x. Cosine of three pi over two plus x is an odd multiple, so it swaps to sine, and the fourth quadrant makes cosine positive, giving sine x. Tangent of pi plus x is tangent x. Cotangent of pi over two minus x swaps to tangent x. The ratio of sine squared to tangent squared is cosine squared.

slides.heading: Domain, range and period
slides.body_md: The **period** of a function is the smallest positive $p$ with $f(x + p) = f(x)$ for all $x$ in the domain.

visual.alt: Table of domain, range and smallest positive period of the six trigonometric functions, with n an integer: sine and cosine are defined everywhere with range minus 1 to 1 and period 2 pi; tangent and secant exclude odd multiples of pi over 2; cotangent and cosecant exclude multiples of pi; tangent and cotangent take all real values with period pi; secant and cosecant have range outside the open interval from minus 1 to 1 and period 2 pi.
visual.caption: Here $n$ is any integer.

slides.narration: This table gathers the facts for all six functions. Sine and cosine are defined everywhere and take values from minus one to one. Tangent and cotangent take every real value. Secant and cosecant never take values between minus one and one. Tangent and cotangent repeat every pi, and the other four repeat every two pi. Tangent and secant fail at odd multiples of pi over two; cotangent and cosecant fail at multiples of pi.

slides.heading: The graph of sine
slides.body_md: $y = \sin x$ is a wave of height $1$ that repeats every $2\pi$; it crosses the axis at every multiple of $\pi$.

visual.alt: The graph of y equal to sine x from minus 6.6 to 6.6: a smooth wave between minus 1 and 1 that crosses the horizontal axis at minus 2 pi, minus pi, 0, pi and 2 pi, with peaks at minus 3 pi over 2 and pi over 2 and troughs at minus pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2.
visual.caption: $y = \sin x$: period $2\pi$, range $[-1, 1]$, zeros at $n\pi$.

slides.narration: The sine graph is a smooth wave. It starts at zero, rises to one at pi over two, returns to zero at pi, falls to minus one at three pi over two, and is back at zero at two pi. Then the pattern repeats in both directions. It is symmetric about the origin, because sine is an odd function, and it crosses the axis at every multiple of pi.

slides.heading: The graph of cosine
slides.body_md: $y = \cos x$ is the sine wave moved $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ to the left; it crosses the axis at the odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

visual.alt: The graph of y equal to cosine x from minus 6.6 to 6.6: the sine wave shifted left by pi over 2, with peaks at minus 2 pi, 0 and 2 pi, troughs at minus pi and pi, and zeros at minus 3 pi over 2, minus pi over 2, pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2.
visual.caption: $y = \cos x$: period $2\pi$, range $[-1, 1]$, zeros at odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

slides.narration: The cosine graph has the same shape as the sine graph, moved left by pi over two. It starts at its highest point, one, crosses the axis at pi over two, reaches its lowest point at pi, crosses again at three pi over two and returns to one at two pi. It is symmetric about the vertical axis, because cosine is an even function.

slides.heading: Quick check: the period of sine and cosine
slides.body_md: Compare the smallest repeating lengths of the two waves.
slides.narration: A half turn changes the sign of both functions, so it is not a period.

slides.heading: The graph of tangent
slides.body_md: $y = \tan x$ has vertical asymptotes at the odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$; between them it rises through every real value. Period $\pi$.

visual.alt: The graph of y equal to tangent x as three separate branches, each rising from the bottom of the picture to the top, between the vertical dashed lines at minus 3 pi over 2, minus pi over 2, pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2. It crosses the horizontal axis at minus pi, 0 and pi and passes through pi over 4, 1 and minus pi over 4, minus 1.
visual.caption: $y = \tan x$: period $\pi$, all real values, asymptotes at odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

slides.narration: Tangent is sine divided by cosine, so it breaks down where cosine is zero, at the odd multiples of pi over two. There the graph has vertical asymptotes. Between two asymptotes it rises from very large negative values to very large positive values, passing through the axis at multiples of pi and through one at pi over four. The same branch repeats every pi.

slides.heading: The graph of cosecant
slides.body_md: $y = \operatorname{cosec} x = \dfrac{1}{\sin x}$ has asymptotes at every multiple of $\pi$ and never takes a value between $-1$ and $1$.

visual.alt: The graph of y equal to cosecant x for x from minus 6.5 to 6.5 as four separate branches between the vertical dashed lines at minus 2 pi, minus pi, 0, pi and 2 pi. Branches above 1 lie over the intervals where sine is positive, with lowest points at minus 3 pi over 2 and pi over 2; branches below minus 1 lie where sine is negative, with highest points at minus pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2.
visual.caption: $y = \operatorname{cosec} x$: never between $-1$ and $1$; asymptotes at $n\pi$.

slides.narration: Cosecant is the reciprocal of sine, so it has asymptotes wherever sine is zero, at the multiples of pi. Where sine is positive the graph is a bowl above one with its lowest point exactly at the peak of the sine wave. Where sine is negative it is an upside down bowl below minus one. The graph repeats every two pi.

slides.heading: The graph of secant
slides.body_md: $y = \sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$ has asymptotes at the odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and never takes a value between $-1$ and $1$.

Branches above 1 have lowest points at minus 2 pi, 0 and 2 pi; branches below minus 1 have highest points at minus pi and pi.
visual.caption: $y = \sec x$: never between $-1$ and $1$; asymptotes at odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

slides.narration: Secant is the reciprocal of cosine. It has asymptotes where cosine is zero, at the odd multiples of pi over two. Where the cosine wave peaks at one, the secant has its lowest point on a bowl above one. Where cosine reaches minus one, secant has the highest point of an upside down bowl. The pattern repeats every two pi.

slides.heading: The graph of cotangent
slides.body_md: $y = \cot x$ has asymptotes at the multiples of $\pi$; between them it **falls** through every real value, crossing the axis at the odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

visual.alt: The graph of y equal to cotangent x for x from minus 6.5 to 6.5 as four branches, each falling from the top of the picture to the bottom between the vertical dashed lines at minus 2 pi, minus pi, 0, pi and 2 pi. It crosses the horizontal axis at minus 3 pi over 2, minus pi over 2, pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2.
visual.caption: $y = \cot x$: period $\pi$, all real values, zeros at odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

slides.narration: Cotangent is cosine divided by sine, so its asymptotes are where sine is zero, at the multiples of pi. Between two asymptotes the graph falls from very large positive values to very large negative values, crossing the axis where cosine is zero, at the odd multiples of pi over two. It repeats every pi, like tangent, but it falls where tangent rises.

slides.narration: Start from the range of cosine, minus one to one. Multiplying by minus two gives minus two to two, and adding three gives one to five. Changing the height or the level of a wave does not change its period, which stays two pi.

notes.title: Angles and Trigonometric Functions - chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Angles and their measures
sections.body_md:
An angle is formed by rotating a ray about its vertex. **Anticlockwise** rotation gives a **positive** angle and **clockwise** rotation a **negative** one; angles with the same terminal side are **coterminal** and differ by whole turns.

A full turn is $360^\circ$ or $2\pi$ radians. A **radian** is the angle at the centre of a circle that cuts off an arc equal to the radius, so $\theta = \dfrac{l}{r}$. Hence $\pi$ radians $= 180^\circ$.

key_terms.definition_md: The angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc equal in length to the radius.
Angles with the same terminal side; they differ by multiples of $360^\circ$.

visual.alt: Table converting common angles from degrees to radians, from 30 degrees equal to pi over 6 up to 360 degrees equal to 2 pi.
visual.caption: $\pi$ radians $= 180^\circ$, so $1^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{180}$ radian and $1$ radian $= \dfrac{180}{\pi}$ degrees.

visuals.alt: A circle with centre O and two radii, one to a point P above the horizontal axis and one to a point N below it. The angle to P is marked plus 50 degrees, turned anticlockwise, and the angle to N is marked minus 50 degrees, turned clockwise from the positive horizontal axis.
visuals.caption: Anticlockwise gives $+50^\circ$; clockwise gives $-50^\circ$.

visuals.alt: A circle sector with centre O and radius r. The arc between the two radii is twice as long as the radius, so the angle at the centre is 2 radians, about 115 degrees.
visuals.caption: An arc of length $2r$ subtends $2$ radians.

sections.heading: 2. Arc length and area of a sector
sections.body_md:
With $\theta$ in **radians**, the arc cut off by the angle $\theta$ in a circle of radius $r$ has length $l = r\theta$, and the sector has area $A = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}rl$.

In degrees: $l = \dfrac{\pi r\theta}{180}$ and $A = \dfrac{\pi r^2\theta}{360}$. The perimeter of a sector is $2r + l$. When both $l$ and $A$ are given, $A = \dfrac{1}{2}rl$ gives $r$ at once.

key_terms.definition_md: The region of a disc bounded by two radii and the arc between them.

visual.alt: Table of sector formulae: arc length is r theta with theta in radians or pi r theta over 180 with theta in degrees; area is half r squared theta or pi r squared theta over 360; and in terms of the arc the area is half r times l.
visual.caption: Same facts in two units; radians give the shorter formulas.

visuals.alt: A circle sector with centre O, radius r and central angle theta. The curved boundary between the two radii has length l, which equals r times theta when theta is measured in radians.
visuals.caption: $l = r\theta$ when $\theta$ is in radians.

visuals.alt: Worked example 3 table: from an arc of 12 centimetres and an area of 36 square centimetres, the radius is 6 centimetres, the angle is 2 radians, which is about 114.59 degrees.
visuals.caption: Both $l$ and $A$ given: solve for $r$ first.

sections.heading: 3. The unit circle and the six functions
sections.body_md: Turn from $(1, 0)$ through $\theta$ on the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ to reach $P$. Then $\cos\theta$ is the $x$-coordinate of $P$ and $\sin\theta$ its $y$-coordinate. The other functions are $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$, $\cot\theta = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$, $\sec\theta = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$ and $\operatorname{cosec}\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$ wherever the denominators are non-zero.

key_terms.definition_md: The circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ with centre at the origin.

visual.alt: The unit circle with a point P in the second quadrant at an angle theta of 125 degrees from the positive horizontal axis, with a dashed vertical line down to the horizontal axis. The coordinates of P are cosine theta and sine theta.
visual.caption: $P(\theta) = (\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta)$; here $\theta = 125^\circ$.

visuals.alt: A circle with its centre O. A radius from O to a point P on the circle makes an angle called theta with the positive horizontal axis; a dashed line drops from P to the horizontal axis.
visuals.caption: Turning from the positive $x$-axis through $\theta$ reaches the point $P$.

sections.heading: 4. Identities and signs in the quadrants
sections.body_md:
Because $P$ lies on the unit circle, $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ for every real $\theta$. Dividing by $\cos^2\theta$ or $\sin^2\theta$ gives $1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$ and $1 + \cot^2\theta = \operatorname{cosec}^2\theta$.

Signs: all functions positive in quadrant I; only sine and cosecant in II; only tangent and cotangent in III; only cosine and secant in IV. To find the other ratios from one, use the identities to get the size, then the quadrant to get the sign. For a proof, work on one side and name each identity you use.

visual.alt: Table of the basic relations: sine squared plus cosine squared equals one for all angles; one plus tangent squared equals secant squared where cosine is not zero; one plus cotangent squared equals cosecant squared where sine is not zero; tangent and cotangent as quotients; cosecant and secant as reciprocals.
visual.caption: All five follow from the unit circle.

visuals.alt: The four quadrants of the coordinate plane with the functions that are positive in each: all six in the first quadrant, sine and cosecant in the second, tangent and cotangent in the third, and cosine and secant in the fourth.
visuals.caption: Positive functions by quadrant; the rest are negative.

rows: $-\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{400}{841}}$, sine is negative in quadrant IV

visuals.alt: Worked example 4 table for cosine theta equal to 20 over 29 in the fourth quadrant: sine is minus 21 over 29, tangent minus 21 over 20, cosecant minus 29 over 21, secant 29 over 20 and cotangent minus 20 over 21.
visuals.caption: Given $\cos\theta = \dfrac{20}{29}$, $\theta$ in quadrant IV.

visuals.alt: Worked example 5 table proving that sine over one plus cosine, plus one plus cosine over sine, equals 2 cosecant: combine over a common denominator, expand, use sine squared plus cosine squared equals one, cancel one plus cosine, and write the result as 2 cosecant theta.
visuals.caption: Start from the left side only.

sections.heading: 5. Functions of any angle
sections.body_md:
Adding or removing whole turns does not change any value: $\sin(\theta + 2n\pi) = \sin\theta$ and so on. To find a value at a large or negative angle, reduce it to $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$, find the quadrant and use the **reference angle**, the acute angle the terminal side makes with the $x$-axis.

Exact values at $0^\circ, 30^\circ, 45^\circ, 60^\circ, 90^\circ$ are in the table; those at other multiples of $15^\circ$ are not needed in this chapter.

key_terms.definition_md: The acute angle between the terminal side and the $x$-axis.

visual.alt: Table of the six trigonometric functions at 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees. Sine runs 0, one half, root 2 over 2, root 3 over 2, 1; cosine runs the other way; tangent runs 0, root 3 over 3, 1, root 3, not defined; and the reciprocal functions follow, with cosecant not defined at 0 and secant and cotangent not defined where their denominators vanish.
visual.caption: Learn sine; the rest follow from it.

visuals.alt: Table reducing large angles by whole turns: 765 degrees is 2 turns plus 45 degrees in the first quadrant; minus 840 degrees is minus 3 turns plus 240 degrees in the third; 1230 degrees is 3 turns plus 150 degrees in the second; 2100 degrees is 5 turns plus 300 degrees in the fourth.
visuals.caption: Adding or removing whole turns does not change any trigonometric value.

sections.heading: 6. Allied angles
sections.body_md:
For an acute $\theta$, the angles $-\theta$, $90^\circ \pm \theta$, $180^\circ \pm \theta$, $270^\circ \pm \theta$ and $360^\circ - \theta$ are called allied angles. **Rule:** for even multiples of $90^\circ$ keep the function; for odd multiples swap sine with cosine, tangent with cotangent and secant with cosecant; the sign is the sign of the original function in the quadrant of the angle.

So $\sin(180^\circ + \theta) = -\sin\theta$, $\cos(90^\circ + \theta) = -\sin\theta$ and $\tan(270^\circ - \theta) = \cot\theta$. Cosine is even; sine and tangent are odd.

key_terms.definition_md: Angles of the form $k \cdot 90^\circ \pm \theta$ whose functions are given by those of $\theta$.

visual.alt: Table of allied-angle results. Minus theta: minus sine theta, cosine theta, minus tangent theta. 90 degrees minus theta: cosine, sine, cotangent. 90 plus theta: cosine, minus sine, minus cotangent. 180 minus theta: sine, minus cosine, minus tangent. 180 plus theta: minus sine, minus cosine, tangent. 270 minus theta: minus cosine, minus sine, cotangent. 270 plus theta: minus cosine, sine, minus cotangent. 360 minus theta: minus sine, cosine, minus tangent.
visual.caption: Here $\theta$ is treated as an acute angle.

visuals.alt: The unit circle with P at angle theta, R at pi minus theta in the second quadrant and S at pi plus theta in the third quadrant. R is the mirror image of P in the vertical axis, and S is the point diametrically opposite P.
visuals.caption: $P(\pi - \theta)$: mirror in the $y$-axis. $P(\pi + \theta)$: opposite end of the diameter.

visuals.alt: The unit circle with a point P at angle theta above the horizontal axis and its mirror image at angle minus theta below it, joined by a dashed vertical line. The two points have the same horizontal position and opposite heights.
visuals.caption: $P(-\theta)$ is the mirror image of $P(\theta)$ in the $x$-axis: $\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta$, $\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 1 table: sine of minus 11 pi over 3 reduces to sine of 60 degrees, which is root 3 over 2; tangent of 1290 degrees reduces to tangent of 210 degrees, which equals tangent of 30 degrees, root 3 over 3; cosine of 1020 degrees reduces to cosine of 300 degrees, which equals cosine of 60 degrees, one half.
visuals.caption: Remove whole turns, then use the allied-angle rule.

even multiple: keep; quadrant III, tangent positive

visuals.caption: Replace each factor, then simplify.

sections.heading: 7. Domain, range, period and graphs
sections.body_md:
Sine and cosine: domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $[-1, 1]$, period $2\pi$. Tangent: domain $\mathbb{R} - \{(2n + 1)\frac{\pi}{2}\}$, range $\mathbb{R}$, period $\pi$. Cotangent: domain $\mathbb{R} - \{n\pi\}$, range $\mathbb{R}$, period $\pi$. Secant and cosecant have range $(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)$ and period $2\pi$; their domains are those of cosine's zeros and sine's zeros respectively.

Sketch the graphs with their asymptotes (dashed): tangent and secant at odd multiples of $\frac{\pi}{2}$, cotangent and cosecant at multiples of $\pi$. For $a + b\cos x$ or $a + b\sin x$, the range is $[a - |b|,\ a + |b|]$.

key_terms.definition_md: The smallest positive $p$ with $f(x + p) = f(x)$ for every $x$ in the domain.
A line that the graph approaches without meeting it, as for $\tan x$ near $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

visual.alt: Table of domain, range and smallest positive period of the six trigonometric functions, with n an integer: sine and cosine are defined everywhere with range minus 1 to 1 and period 2 pi; tangent and secant exclude odd multiples of pi over 2; cotangent and cosecant exclude multiples of pi; tangent and cotangent take all real values with period pi; secant and cosecant have range outside the open interval from minus 1 to 1 and period 2 pi.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are usually awarded**
- *Convert angles (2 marks):* a mark per conversion.
- *Arc and sector (3 marks):* the angle in radians, the formula, then the answer.
- *All ratios from one (3 marks):* the missing ratio, the signs by quadrant, then the rest.
- *Prove an identity (3 marks):* start from one side, the key identity, the finish.
- *Exact value of a large angle (2-3 marks):* the reduction line, the allied step, the value.
- *Domain, range, period (2-3 marks):* a mark for each.
- *Sketch (3 marks):* shape, key points, asymptotes or intercepts.
- *Section D (5 marks):* questions come in parts such as 2 + 3; label each part.

**Common mistakes**
- Using $l = r\theta$ with $\theta$ in degrees.
- Choosing the sign of a ratio before naming the quadrant.
- Writing $\sin(\pi + x) = \sin x$ or forgetting to swap the function for odd multiples of $90^\circ$.
- Saying that $\sec x$ can take values between $-1$ and $1$.
- Treating $\tan x$ as defined at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.stem_md: By convention, an angle formed by turning the initial ray in the clockwise sense is called
questions.solution_md: Anticlockwise rotation gives positive angles and clockwise rotation gives negative angles. A reflex angle is one between $180^\circ$ and $360^\circ$, and a quadrantal angle is a multiple of $90^\circ$; neither describes the sense of the turn.

questions.stem_md: Converted into radians, the angle $-72^\circ$ becomes
questions.solution_md: Multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$: $-72 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = -\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$. Dividing by $360$ instead gives $-\dfrac{\pi}{5}$, and dropping the sign gives $\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$.

questions.stem_md: An arc of length $4.2$ m is cut from a circle of radius $1.5$ m. The angle it subtends at the centre of the circle is
questions.solution_md: With $l = r\theta$, $\theta = \dfrac{l}{r} = \dfrac{4.2}{1.5} = 2.8$ radians. The product $6.3$ multiplies instead of dividing, and $5.7$ adds the two lengths.

questions.stem_md: A sector of a circle has radius $12$ cm and central angle $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$. Its area, in square centimetres, is
questions.solution_md: $A = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 144 \times \dfrac{5\pi}{6} = 60\pi$. Omitting the factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$ gives $120\pi$; the value $10\pi$ is the arc length $r\theta$.

questions.stem_md: The hour hand of a wall clock moves from the $3$ o'clock position to the $7{:}30$ position. The angle it turns through is
questions.solution_md: The hour hand turns $30^\circ$ in each hour, so in $4.5$ hours it turns $4.5 \times 30^\circ = 135^\circ = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ radians. Counting only $4$ hours gives $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

questions.stem_md: Given $\sin\theta = -\dfrac{3}{5}$ and $\cos\theta > 0$, the value of $\tan\theta$ is
questions.solution_md: The cosine is positive, so $\cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{9}{25}} = \dfrac{4}{5}$. Then $\tan\theta = \dfrac{-3/5}{4/5} = -\dfrac{3}{4}$. The reciprocal $-\dfrac{4}{3}$ is $\cot\theta$.

questions.stem_md: The terminal side of an angle of $5$ radians lies in
questions.solution_md: Since $\dfrac{3\pi}{2} \approx 4.71$ and $2\pi \approx 6.28$, the angle $5$ lies between them, so the terminal side is in the fourth quadrant, where sine is negative and cosine is positive.

questions.stem_md: Wherever the expressions are defined, $1 + \cot^2\theta$ is identical to
questions.solution_md: Divide $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ by $\sin^2\theta$: $1 + \cot^2\theta = \operatorname{cosec}^2\theta$. The companion identity $1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$ is the one that gives the wrong option $\sec^2\theta$.

questions.stem_md: Exactly one of the numbers below can be the value of $\sec\theta$ for some real angle $\theta$. Which one?
questions.solution_md: Since $\sec\theta = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$ and $-1 \le \cos\theta \le 1$, we need $|\sec\theta| \ge 1$. Only $-\dfrac{5}{4}$ qualifies, with $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{4}{5}$. A reciprocal is never $0$.

questions.stem_md: If $\tan\theta = -\dfrac{5}{12}$ and $\sin\theta > 0$, then $\cos\theta$ equals
questions.solution_md: A negative tangent with a positive sine puts $\theta$ in the second quadrant, where cosine is negative. With legs $5$ and $12$ the hypotenuse is $13$, so $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{12}{13}$.

questions.stem_md: If $\sin\theta - \cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{3}$, then the product $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ equals
questions.solution_md: Square both sides: $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta - 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{9}$, so $1 - 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{9}$ and $\sin\theta\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{9}\right) = \dfrac{4}{9}$. Forgetting the factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$ gives $\dfrac{8}{9}$.

questions.stem_md: The expression $\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} - x\right)$ can be rewritten, for any real $x$, as
questions.solution_md: The angle $\dfrac{3\pi}{2} - x$ lies in the third quadrant for small positive $x$, where sine is negative, and an odd multiple of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ turns sine into cosine. So $\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} - x\right) = -\cos x$.

questions.stem_md: The exact value of $\cos 570^\circ$ is
questions.solution_md: Subtract one full turn: $570^\circ - 360^\circ = 210^\circ$, a third-quadrant angle with reference angle $30^\circ$. Cosine is negative there, so $\cos 570^\circ = -\cos 30^\circ = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

questions.stem_md: The value of $\tan\left(-\dfrac{13\pi}{6}\right)$ is
questions.solution_md: $-\dfrac{13\pi}{6} = -390^\circ = -360^\circ - 30^\circ$, so the angle is coterminal with $-30^\circ$. Tangent is odd, so $\tan(-30^\circ) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$.

questions.stem_md: The exact value of the product $\sin 330^\circ \cdot \cos 150^\circ$ is
questions.solution_md: $\sin 330^\circ = -\sin 30^\circ = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $\cos 150^\circ = -\cos 30^\circ = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. The product of the two negative numbers is $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$.

questions.stem_md: In a triangle $ABC$, the quantity $\cos(A + B) + \cos C$ always equals
questions.solution_md: The angles of a triangle add up to $\pi$, so $A + B = \pi - C$ and $\cos(A + B) = \cos(\pi - C) = -\cos C$. Adding $\cos C$ gives $0$.

questions.stem_md: As $x$ runs over all real numbers, the function $f(x) = 4 - 3\sin x$ takes exactly the values in
questions.solution_md: Since $-1 \le \sin x \le 1$, we get $-3 \le -3\sin x \le 3$ and hence $1 \le 4 - 3\sin x \le 7$; both ends occur at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.stem_md: The cotangent function $\cot x$ is defined for every real $x$ except those of the form
questions.solution_md: $\cot x = \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$ fails exactly where $\sin x = 0$, that is at every integer multiple of $\pi$. The odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ are where $\tan x$ fails.

questions.stem_md: Which of these functions has the set $(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)$ as its range?
questions.solution_md: Because $|\sin x| \le 1$ and $\operatorname{cosec} x = \dfrac{1}{\sin x}$, we have $|\operatorname{cosec} x| \ge 1$, and every such value occurs. Tangent and cotangent take every real value; sine stays within $[-1, 1]$.

questions.stem_md: For $0 \le x \le 4\pi$, the graph of $y = \sin x$ meets the horizontal line $y = \dfrac{1}{2}$ at how many points?
questions.solution_md: In each complete wave of length $2\pi$ the sine curve rises through $\dfrac{1}{2}$ once, at $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and falls through it once, at $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$. Two waves give $2 \times 2 = 4$ points.

questions.stem_md: How many vertical asymptotes does the graph of $y = \cot x$ have in the closed interval $-2\pi \le x \le 2\pi$?
questions.solution_md: The asymptotes are at the zeros of $\sin x$, the integer multiples of $\pi$: $-2\pi, -\pi, 0, \pi, 2\pi$. Counting both end points of the closed interval gives $5$.

questions.stem_md: After how large an increase in $x$ does the graph of $f(x) = \cos\dfrac{x}{3}$ first repeat itself? That least positive length is
questions.solution_md: $\cos\theta$ repeats when $\theta$ grows by $2\pi$. Here $\theta = \dfrac{x}{3}$, so $x$ must grow by $3 \times 2\pi = 6\pi$. The value $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ would belong to $\cos 3x$.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. On the unit circle, turning by $-x$ gives the mirror image in the horizontal axis, which flips the sign of the height; that is A. The period in R is a different property and does not lead to A.

questions.stem_md: The identity $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ holds for every real $\theta$, including those where $\tan\theta$ is undefined.
questions.solution_md: The identity is Pythagoras' theorem for the point $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ on the unit circle; it needs no division, so it also holds at $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, where $\tan\theta$ is undefined.

questions.stem_md: The angle $400^\circ$ and the angle $-320^\circ$ have the same terminal side.
questions.solution_md: Subtracting one turn, $400^\circ - 360^\circ = 40^\circ$; adding one turn, $-320^\circ + 360^\circ = 40^\circ$. Both end where $40^\circ$ ends.

questions.stem_md: The smallest positive period of the sine function and of the cosine function is the same number, $2\pi$.
questions.solution_md: Both curves repeat after one full turn and not before: $\sin(x + 2\pi) = \sin x$ and $\cos(x + 2\pi) = \cos x$, while a half turn changes the sign of each.

questions.stem_md: The graph of $y = \sec x$ crosses the $x$-axis at some points.
questions.solution_md: $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$ is a reciprocal, so it is never $0$; in fact $|\sec x| \ge 1$. The graph has branches above $y = 1$ and below $y = -1$ and never touches the axis.

questions.stem_md: When a central angle of $1$ radian is drawn in two circles of different radii, the larger circle gives the larger radian measure for that angle.
questions.solution_md: Radian measure is the ratio $\dfrac{\text{arc}}{\text{radius}}$. Doubling the radius doubles the arc cut off by the same angle, so the ratio stays $1$. The measure does not depend on the circle.

questions.stem_md: An angle exists for which $\tan\theta = 100$ and $\operatorname{cosec}\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$ at the same time.
questions.solution_md: The condition $\operatorname{cosec}\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$ needs $\sin\theta = 2$, which is impossible because $|\sin\theta| \le 1$. So no angle satisfies both, whatever happens with the tangent.

questions.stem_md: In degrees, the angle $\dfrac{11\pi}{12}$ radians measures ____.
questions.solution_md: Multiply by $\dfrac{180}{\pi}$: $\dfrac{11\pi}{12} \times \dfrac{180}{\pi} = 165$, that is $165^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A circle has radius $12$ cm. An angle of $0.75$ radian at its centre cuts off an arc of length ____ cm.
questions.solution_md: $l = r\theta = 12 \times 0.75 = 9$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The value of $\operatorname{cosec}\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ is ____.
questions.solution_md: $\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -1$, so its reciprocal $\operatorname{cosec}\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{-1} = -1$.

questions.stem_md: The number of integers that belong to the range of $f(x) = 5\sin x - 2$ is ____.
questions.solution_md: From $-1 \le \sin x \le 1$ we get $-7 \le 5\sin x - 2 \le 3$, and every value in $[-7, 3]$ occurs. The integers $-7, -6, \dots, 3$ number $11$.

questions.stem_md: A turntable completes $3\dfrac{1}{2}$ full turns in the anticlockwise sense. The angle it has turned through is ____ $\pi$ radians.
questions.solution_md: Each full turn is $2\pi$ radians, so $3.5 \times 2\pi = 7\pi$ radians.

questions.stem_md: The value of $\cos 540^\circ$ is ____.
questions.solution_md: $540^\circ = 360^\circ + 180^\circ$, so $\cos 540^\circ = \cos 180^\circ = -1$.

questions.stem_md: A runner follows a circular bend of radius $2.5$ m through a central angle of $132^\circ$. Find the length of the bend in metres, correct to two decimal places (use $\pi = 3.14159$).
questions.solution_md: $\theta = 132 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = 2.3038$ radians, so $l = r\theta = 2.5 \times 2.3038 = 5.76$ m.

questions.stem_md: A sector with central angle $0.8$ radian has area $25.6$ cm$^2$. Find the radius of the circle in centimetres.
questions.solution_md: From $A = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$: $25.6 = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2 \times 0.8$, so $r^2 = \dfrac{25.6}{0.4} = 64$ and $r = 8$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The boundary of a sector consists of an arc $13$ cm long and two radii of $8$ cm each. Find the area of the sector in square centimetres.
questions.solution_md: For a sector, $A = \dfrac{1}{2}rl = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 13 = 52$ cm$^2$.

questions.stem_md: The angle $\theta$ lies in the third quadrant and $\cot\theta = \dfrac{15}{8}$. Find $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$ as a decimal.
questions.solution_md: $1 + \cot^2\theta = 1 + \dfrac{225}{64} = \dfrac{289}{64}$, so $|\operatorname{cosec}\theta| = \dfrac{17}{8}$. Sine is negative in the third quadrant, so $\operatorname{cosec}\theta = -\dfrac{17}{8} = -2.125$.

questions.stem_md: A turning arm has rotated through $2.4$ radians. State this angle in degrees, correct to two decimal places (take $\pi = 3.14159$).
Suppose $\sec\theta - \tan\theta = \dfrac{2}{5}$. Determine the numerical value of $\sec\theta + \tan\theta$, written as a decimal.
questions.solution_md: Since $\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1$, we have $(\sec\theta - \tan\theta)(\sec\theta + \tan\theta) = 1$. So $\sec\theta + \tan\theta = 1 \div \dfrac{2}{5} = 2.5$.

questions.stem_md: Express $56^\circ$ in radians, and express $\dfrac{13\pi}{20}$ radians in degrees.

answer.model_answer_md: $56^\circ = 56 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{14\pi}{45}$ radians. $\dfrac{13\pi}{20}$ radians $= \dfrac{13\pi}{20} \times \dfrac{180}{\pi} = 117^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$ going to radians and by $\dfrac{180}{\pi}$ coming back.

questions.stem_md: A pendulum bob swings along an arc of length $22$ cm at the end of a string $90$ cm long. Find the angle of swing, in radians and in degrees (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).

answer.model_answer_md: $\theta = \dfrac{l}{r} = \dfrac{22}{90} = \dfrac{11}{45}$ radian. In degrees, $\dfrac{11}{45} \times \dfrac{180}{\pi} = \dfrac{11}{45} \times 180 \times \dfrac{7}{22} = 14^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Divide the arc by the radius, then convert with the given value of $\pi$.

questions.stem_md: The number $4$ is an angle measured in radians. State, with a reason, the signs of $\sin 4$, $\cos 4$ and $\tan 4$.

answer.model_answer_md: Since $\pi \approx 3.14$ and $\dfrac{3\pi}{2} \approx 4.71$, the angle $4$ lies between $\pi$ and $\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, in the third quadrant. There $\sin 4 < 0$, $\cos 4 < 0$ and $\tan 4 > 0$ (a negative divided by a negative).

questions.solution_md: Locate the angle between two quadrantal values first.

questions.stem_md: The angle $\theta$ lies in the second quadrant and $\tan\theta = -\dfrac{7}{24}$. Find $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$.

answer.model_answer_md: Legs $7$ and $24$ give hypotenuse $\sqrt{49 + 576} = 25$. In the second quadrant sine is positive and cosine is negative, so $\sin\theta = \dfrac{7}{25}$ and $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{24}{25}$.

questions.solution_md: Build the right triangle from the tangent, then attach signs by quadrant.

questions.stem_md: Prove that $\sin^4\theta - \cos^4\theta = \sin^2\theta - \cos^2\theta$.

answer.model_answer_md: The left side is a difference of squares: $\sin^4\theta - \cos^4\theta = (\sin^2\theta - \cos^2\theta)(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta)$. Since $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$, this equals $\sin^2\theta - \cos^2\theta$, the right side.

questions.solution_md: Factorise as a difference of squares and use the Pythagorean identity.

questions.stem_md: Show that $\dfrac{\cos\theta}{1 - \sin\theta} = \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ wherever both sides are defined.

answer.model_answer_md: Cross-multiplying, we need $\cos^2\theta = (1 - \sin\theta)(1 + \sin\theta) = 1 - \sin^2\theta$. This is true because $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$. Hence the two sides are equal.

questions.solution_md: Cross-multiply and recognise a difference of squares.

questions.stem_md: Find the exact value of $\sin 240^\circ \cdot \tan 315^\circ$.

answer.model_answer_md: $240^\circ$ is in the third quadrant with reference angle $60^\circ$, so $\sin 240^\circ = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. $315^\circ$ is in the fourth quadrant with reference angle $45^\circ$, so $\tan 315^\circ = -1$. The product is $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

questions.stem_md: Evaluate $\sin\left(-\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) + \cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ without a calculator.

answer.model_answer_md: $\sin\left(-\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = -\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{6} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$, since $\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{6} = \sin\left(\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Also $\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3} = -\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$. The sum is $-1$.

questions.solution_md: Use oddness of sine and the allied-angle results for $\pi \pm \theta$.

questions.stem_md: State the domain, the range and the smallest positive period of the function $y = \sec x$.

answer.model_answer_md: Domain: all real $x$ except the odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, where $\cos x = 0$. Range: $(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)$, because $|\cos x| \le 1$. Period: $2\pi$, since $\sec(x + \pi) = -\sec x$ shows that $\pi$ is too short.

questions.solution_md: Work from $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$.

questions.stem_md: For $0 \le x \le 2\pi$, find the least and the greatest value of $f(x) = 5 - 4\cos x$, and a value of $x$ at which each is reached.

answer.model_answer_md: Since $-1 \le \cos x \le 1$, we have $1 \le 5 - 4\cos x \le 9$. The least value $1$ occurs when $\cos x = 1$, that is at $x = 0$ (and again at $x = 2\pi$). The greatest value $9$ occurs when $\cos x = -1$, at $x = \pi$.

questions.solution_md: Bound $\cos x$ and read off the two extremes.

questions.stem_md: A circular saw blade turns at $480$ revolutions per minute. Through what angle does it turn in $5$ seconds? Give the answer in radians (as a multiple of $\pi$) and in degrees.

answer.model_answer_md: $480$ revolutions per minute is $\dfrac{480}{60} = 8$ revolutions per second, so in $5$ seconds the blade makes $8 \times 5 = 40$ revolutions. Each revolution is $2\pi$ radians, so the angle is $40 \times 2\pi = 80\pi$ radians. In degrees this is $40 \times 360^\circ = 14400^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Count the revolutions first, then convert at $2\pi$ radians or $360^\circ$ per revolution.

questions.stem_md: A sector of a circle of radius $15$ cm has a perimeter of $51$ cm. Find its arc length, its central angle in radians and its area.

answer.model_answer_md: The perimeter is two radii plus the arc, so the arc length is $l = 51 - 2 \times 15 = 21$ cm. The angle is $\theta = \dfrac{l}{r} = \dfrac{21}{15} = 1.4$ radians. The area is $\dfrac{1}{2}rl = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 15 \times 21 = 157.5$ cm$^2$.

questions.solution_md: Subtract the radii from the perimeter, then use $\theta = \dfrac{l}{r}$ and $A = \dfrac{1}{2}rl$.

questions.stem_md: The angle $\theta$ lies in the third quadrant and $\cot\theta = \dfrac{15}{8}$. Find $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$ and $\sec\theta$.

answer.model_answer_md: The legs are $15$ and $8$, so the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{225 + 64} = 17$. In the third quadrant sine and cosine are both negative, so $\sin\theta = -\dfrac{8}{17}$ and $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{15}{17}$. Then $\sec\theta = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} = -\dfrac{17}{15}$.

questions.solution_md: Draw the reference triangle and use the sign pattern of the third quadrant.

questions.stem_md: Prove that $(\operatorname{cosec}\theta - \cot\theta)^2 = \dfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{1 + \cos\theta}$.

answer.model_answer_md: $(\operatorname{cosec}\theta - \cot\theta)^2 = \left(\dfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\right)^2 = \dfrac{(1 - \cos\theta)^2}{\sin^2\theta}$. Replace $\sin^2\theta$ by $1 - \cos^2\theta = (1 - \cos\theta)(1 + \cos\theta)$. Cancelling the common factor $1 - \cos\theta$ leaves $\dfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{1 + \cos\theta}$.

questions.solution_md: Write everything with sine and cosine, then factorise the denominator.

questions.stem_md: Prove that $\tan^2\theta - \sin^2\theta = \tan^2\theta\,\sin^2\theta$.

answer.model_answer_md: Left side: $\tan^2\theta - \sin^2\theta = \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} - \sin^2\theta = \sin^2\theta\left(\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta} - 1\right)$. Now $\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta} - 1 = \dfrac{1 - \cos^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} = \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} = \tan^2\theta$. Hence the left side is $\sin^2\theta\tan^2\theta$.

questions.solution_md: Take $\sin^2\theta$ out as a common factor.

questions.stem_md: Find the exact value of $\sin 750^\circ + \cos(-300^\circ)\tan 225^\circ$.

answer.model_answer_md: $\sin 750^\circ = \sin(720^\circ + 30^\circ) = \sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Cosine is even, so $\cos(-300^\circ) = \cos 300^\circ = \cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Also $\tan 225^\circ = \tan 45^\circ = 1$. The value is $\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1 = 1$.

questions.solution_md: Reduce each angle by whole turns or half turns, then add the exact values.

questions.stem_md: Simplify $\dfrac{\sin(\pi + x)\,\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + x\right)\tan\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} - x\right)}{\cos(2\pi - x)\,\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + x\right)}$.

answer.model_answer_md: Numerator: $\sin(\pi + x) = -\sin x$, $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + x\right) = -\sin x$ and $\tan\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} - x\right) = \cot x$, so it equals $\sin^2 x\cot x = \sin x\cos x$. Denominator: $\cos(2\pi - x) = \cos x$ and $\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + x\right) = -\cos x$, so it equals $-\cos^2 x$. The quotient is $\dfrac{\sin x\cos x}{-\cos^2 x} = -\tan x$.

questions.solution_md: Replace each factor by an allied-angle result, collect the signs, then simplify.

questions.stem_md: Without tables, show that $\sin^2 28^\circ + \sin^2 62^\circ + \tan^2 45^\circ = 2$.

answer.model_answer_md: Since $62^\circ = 90^\circ - 28^\circ$, we have $\sin 62^\circ = \cos 28^\circ$. So $\sin^2 28^\circ + \sin^2 62^\circ = \sin^2 28^\circ + \cos^2 28^\circ = 1$. Also $\tan 45^\circ = 1$, so $\tan^2 45^\circ = 1$. The total is $1 + 1 = 2$.

questions.solution_md: Complementary angles turn sine into cosine.

questions.stem_md: For the function $y = \cot x$, state the domain, the range, the smallest positive period, the equations of its vertical asymptotes for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$, and the values of $x$ in $(0, 2\pi)$ where it is zero.

answer.model_answer_md: $\cot x = \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$. Domain: all real $x$ except $x = n\pi$; range: all real numbers; period: $\pi$, because $\cot(x + \pi) = \cot x$. Asymptotes for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$: $x = 0$, $x = \pi$ and $x = 2\pi$, where $\sin x = 0$. Zeros in $(0, 2\pi)$: $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, where $\cos x = 0$.

questions.solution_md: Zeros of the numerator give zeros of the function; zeros of the denominator give asymptotes.

questions.stem_md: Find the range of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{3 - 2\sin x}$.

answer.model_answer_md: Since $-1 \le \sin x \le 1$, we get $-2 \le -2\sin x \le 2$ and so $1 \le 3 - 2\sin x \le 5$. The denominator is always positive, and taking reciprocals reverses the order: $\dfrac{1}{5} \le f(x) \le 1$. The ends are reached when $\sin x = -1$ and $\sin x = 1$, so the range is $\left[\dfrac{1}{5}, 1\right]$.

questions.stem_md: In a triangle $ABC$ prove that $\sin\dfrac{A + B}{2} = \cos\dfrac{C}{2}$.

answer.model_answer_md: The angles of a triangle add up to $\pi$, so $A + B = \pi - C$ and $\dfrac{A + B}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{C}{2}$. Therefore $\sin\dfrac{A + B}{2} = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{C}{2}\right)$. A complementary angle turns sine into cosine, so this equals $\cos\dfrac{C}{2}$.

questions.solution_md: Replace $A + B$ by $\pi - C$ and use the complementary-angle result.

questions.stem_md: At $8{:}20$ the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock make an angle at the centre of the dial. Find this angle in degrees and in radians.

answer.model_answer_md: The minute hand is at $20 \times 6^\circ = 120^\circ$ from the $12$ mark. The hour hand has turned $8 \times 30^\circ + \dfrac{20}{60} \times 30^\circ = 240^\circ + 10^\circ = 250^\circ$. The angle between them is $250^\circ - 120^\circ = 130^\circ$, which is $130 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{13\pi}{18}$ radians.

questions.solution_md: Find each hand's position from the $12$ mark and subtract.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Express $-135^\circ$ in radians and $\dfrac{7\pi}{12}$ radians in degrees. [2]

(b) The rim of an imagined Ferris wheel has radius $21$ m. A passenger cabin travels $33$ m along the rim. Find the angle through which the wheel turns, in radians and in degrees (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$). [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $-135^\circ = -135 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ radians. $\dfrac{7\pi}{12}$ radians $= \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \times \dfrac{180}{\pi} = 105^\circ$.

(b) The angle in radians is $\theta = \dfrac{l}{r} = \dfrac{33}{21} = \dfrac{11}{7}$. To convert, $\dfrac{11}{7} \times \dfrac{180}{\pi} = \dfrac{11}{7} \times 180 \times \dfrac{7}{22} = 90$. So the wheel turns through $\dfrac{11}{7}$ radians, which is $90^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Use $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$ and $\dfrac{180}{\pi}$ for the conversions and $\theta = \dfrac{l}{r}$ for the arc.

questions.stem_md:
A sector of a circle has area $24$ cm$^2$ and perimeter $20$ cm. Let its radius be $r$ cm and its arc length $l$ cm.

(a) Write down two equations connecting $r$ and $l$. [2]

(b) Eliminate $l$ and solve for $r$. [2]

(c) Find the central angle in radians for each value of $r$. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The perimeter gives $2r + l = 20$, and the area gives $\dfrac{1}{2}rl = 24$, that is $rl = 48$.

(b) From the first equation $l = 20 - 2r$, so $r(20 - 2r) = 48$, which simplifies to $r^2 - 10r + 24 = 0$, that is $(r - 4)(r - 6) = 0$. Hence $r = 4$ or $r = 6$.

(c) For $r = 4$: $l = 12$ and $\theta = \dfrac{12}{4} = 3$ radians. For $r = 6$: $l = 8$ and $\theta = \dfrac{8}{6} = \dfrac{4}{3}$ radians. Both satisfy the area, since $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 12 = 24$ and $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 8 = 24$.

questions.solution_md: Two conditions on $r$ and $l$ give a quadratic in $r$ with two admissible roots.

questions.stem_md:
The point $P(\theta)$ of the unit circle, reached by turning through the angle $\theta$ from the point $(1, 0)$, lies in the third quadrant and has $y$-coordinate $-\dfrac{9}{41}$.

(a) Find its $x$-coordinate, and then $\tan\theta$, $\cot\theta$, $\sec\theta$ and $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$. [3]

(b) Find $\sin(\pi + \theta)$, $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + \theta\right)$ and $\tan(2\pi - \theta)$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The coordinates of $P$ are $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ and lie on $x^2 + y^2 = 1$. So $x^2 = 1 - \dfrac{81}{1681} = \dfrac{1600}{1681}$, and $x = -\dfrac{40}{41}$ in the third quadrant. Then $\tan\theta = \dfrac{-9/41}{-40/41} = \dfrac{9}{40}$, $\cot\theta = \dfrac{40}{9}$, $\sec\theta = -\dfrac{41}{40}$ and $\operatorname{cosec}\theta = -\dfrac{41}{9}$.

(b) $\sin(\pi + \theta) = -\sin\theta = \dfrac{9}{41}$. $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + \theta\right) = -\sin\theta = \dfrac{9}{41}$. $\tan(2\pi - \theta) = -\tan\theta = -\dfrac{9}{40}$.

questions.solution_md: Use $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ for the missing coordinate and the allied-angle rules for part (b).

questions.stem_md:
(a) Prove that $\dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{1 - \sin\theta} = (\sec\theta + \tan\theta)^2$. [3]

(b) If $\sec\theta + \tan\theta = 3$, use the identity $\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1$ to find $\sec\theta - \tan\theta$, and hence find $\sin\theta$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Start with the right side: $(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)^2 = \dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta)^2}{\cos^2\theta}$. Replace $\cos^2\theta$ by $1 - \sin^2\theta = (1 - \sin\theta)(1 + \sin\theta)$. Cancelling $1 + \sin\theta$ gives $\dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{1 - \sin\theta}$, the left side.

(b) Since $(\sec\theta - \tan\theta)(\sec\theta + \tan\theta) = 1$, we get $\sec\theta - \tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{3}$. Adding and subtracting the two equations, $2\sec\theta = 3 + \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{10}{3}$ and $2\tan\theta = 3 - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{8}{3}$. So $\sec\theta = \dfrac{5}{3}$ and $\tan\theta = \dfrac{4}{3}$, and $\sin\theta = \tan\theta\cos\theta = \dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{3}{5} = \dfrac{4}{5}$.

questions.solution_md: Express the right side through sine and cosine for (a); the product of the two combinations is $1$ in (b).

questions.stem_md:
(a) Find the exact values of $\sin 1140^\circ$, $\cos(-1305^\circ)$ and $\tan 1125^\circ$. [3]

(b) Simplify $\dfrac{\sin(\pi + x)\,\cos(\pi - x)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + x\right)\cos\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} - x\right)}$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $1140^\circ = 3 \times 360^\circ + 60^\circ$, so $\sin 1140^\circ = \sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Cosine is even and $1305^\circ = 3 \times 360^\circ + 225^\circ$, so $\cos(-1305^\circ) = \cos 225^\circ = -\cos 45^\circ = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$. Also $1125^\circ = 3 \times 360^\circ + 45^\circ$, so $\tan 1125^\circ = 1$.

(b) Numerator: $\sin(\pi + x) = -\sin x$ and $\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x$, giving $\sin x\cos x$. Denominator: $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + x\right) = \cos x$ and $\cos\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} - x\right) = -\sin x$, giving $-\sin x\cos x$. The quotient is $-1$.

questions.solution_md: Remove whole turns first in (a); in (b) replace each factor with an allied-angle result.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Numerator $\sin x\cos x$ and denominator $-\sin x\cos x$

questions.stem_md:
The figure shows the graphs of $y = \cos x$ and $y = \sec x$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.

(a) Write down the equations of the vertical asymptotes of $y = \sec x$ in this interval. [1]

(b) State the range of $\sec x$. [1]

(c) Show that $\sec x = \cos x$ only where $\cos^2 x = 1$, and list the values of $x$ in $[0, 2\pi]$ at which the curves meet. [2]

(d) Find the value of $x$ in $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ for which $\sec x = 2$. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$ is undefined where $\cos x = 0$, so the asymptotes in $[0, 2\pi]$ are $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.

(b) Because $|\cos x| \le 1$, $|\sec x| \ge 1$, so the range is $(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)$.

(c) If $\dfrac{1}{\cos x} = \cos x$, then $\cos^2 x = 1$, so $\cos x = \pm 1$. In $[0, 2\pi]$ this happens at $x = 0$, $x = \pi$ and $x = 2\pi$, giving the points $(0, 1)$, $(\pi, -1)$ and $(2\pi, 1)$ seen in the figure.

(d) $\sec x = 2$ means $\cos x = \dfrac{1}{2}$, and in $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ this gives $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

questions.solution_md: Everything follows from $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$ and $|\cos x| \le 1$.

questions.stem_md:
(a) For each of the functions $\tan x$, $\cot x$, $\sec x$ and $\operatorname{cosec} x$, state the domain and the range. [4]

(b) Use the range of $\operatorname{cosec} x$ to find the range of $y = 2 - \operatorname{cosec} x$. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\tan x$: domain all real $x$ except odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$; range all real numbers. $\cot x$: domain all real $x$ except multiples of $\pi$; range all real numbers. $\sec x$: domain all real $x$ except odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$; range $(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)$. $\operatorname{cosec} x$: domain all real $x$ except multiples of $\pi$; range $(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)$.

(b) We have $\operatorname{cosec} x \le -1$ or $\operatorname{cosec} x \ge 1$. Then $-\operatorname{cosec} x \ge 1$ or $-\operatorname{cosec} x \le -1$, and adding $2$: $y \ge 3$ or $y \le 1$. The range is $(-\infty, 1] \cup [3, \infty)$; the values $1$ and $3$ occur at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.

questions.solution_md: Each domain comes from the zeros of the denominator, each range from $|\sin x| \le 1$ or $|\cos x| \le 1$.

questions.stem_md:
A wiper arm of an imagined bus pivots at a point $O$. Its blade runs from $30$ cm to $48$ cm away from $O$ and sweeps through an angle of $110^\circ$ across the windscreen. Use $\pi = 3.14159$ where a decimal is needed.

(a) Express the angle of the sweep in radians. [1]

(b) Find the lengths of the arcs traced by the outer end and by the inner end of the blade. [2]

(c) Find the area of the windscreen cleaned by the blade. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $110^\circ = 110 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{11\pi}{18}$ radians.

(b) With $l = r\theta$, the outer end traces $48 \times \dfrac{11\pi}{18} = \dfrac{88\pi}{3} \approx 92.15$ cm, and the inner end traces $30 \times \dfrac{11\pi}{18} = \dfrac{55\pi}{3} \approx 57.60$ cm.

(c) The cleaned region is the difference of two sectors with the same angle: $\dfrac{1}{2}\theta(48^2 - 30^2) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{11\pi}{18} \times 1404 = 429\pi \approx 1347.74$ cm$^2$.

questions.solution_md: Treat the cleaned region as the large sector minus the small sector with the same angle.
